result:
The final pick, `final.py` (candidate c23), is valid on the official scorer with a **search score of 66.9**, using **8 of 24 calls**. That number has a large error bar: the scorer's results move by about ±50% with load on this shared laptop. The same file (c19, which differs from the final only by a guard for rare huge-record inputs) scored 114.6 at one point and 72.0 at another. The reference took 2.4 s in one run and 6.4 s in another. So I used the scorer to check validity and ranked candidates with a local A/B timer that alternates them in one process.

| | search (official) | held-out (my harness, seeds 1000+) |
|---|---|---|
| baseline | ~1.0 | 1.0 |
| first champion c1 | 61.7 | 49.1 (one run) |
| final c23 | 66.9 (72.0 and 114.6 for c19) | 67.3 / 66.3 / 61.7 |

**Why it's faster.** It produces exactly the reference's pairs without comparing every pair:
- **Identical records are grouped first.** All their pairs come out at once, and each distinct set is handled only once.
- **Sets of 1–3 words are skipped.** They can only match a set identical to them.
- **Each set is checked only against likely matches.** Words are ranked rarest-first. Two sets at least 80% alike must share a word among each set's first few rarest words, so each set looks up only those words in an index. It also only considers partners with at least 80% of its size.
- **Overlaps are counted with bitmasks when there are many to check.** When a set has 8 or more possible partners, overlaps are counted on integer bitmasks instead of by intersecting Python sets. This took 25–30% off the long-record inputs.
- **No slow or rejected imports.** It counts word frequency on every third set in plain Python, since the order only has to be consistent. That avoids importing `collections` (1–4 ms per run) and `bisect`.
- **Few, huge records are compared directly.** With 2 records of about 100k words, the indexed version was 3.0x slower than the reference, which is at the cutoff. With the guard it now matches the reference.

**Approaches tried:**
- **Prefix filtering** (c1–c3, c5): this was the big step, about 60x.
- **Ordering words by hash instead of frequency** (c4): 12x more pairs to check; dropped.
- **Bitmask checks:** on every pair (c9) they slowed short records; only for long sets (c10) they were mixed; triggered by many candidates (c12, c19) they helped and were kept.
- **Position-based pruning** (c11): halved the pairs to check on long records but cost more than it saved; dropped.
- **Size limit per word position** (c21): 10% fewer pairs to check, same time; dropped.
- **Bulk C-level checking** (c20): no measurable change; dropped.
- **Plain-Python micro-optimizations** (c14–c18, c22, c24, c25): all within noise.

**Correctness and awkward inputs.** Each candidate passed 300 small randomized cases against the reference. The final pick is exact, and never slower than the reference, on:
- all-empty input;
- 3,000 identical records (4.5M pairs);
- nested subsets;
- 100k-word records;
- unusual Unicode whitespace;
- an 8-word vocabulary.

**Two process slips.**
- One scorer call was wasted: c13 imported from `_collections`, and the static check rejects that.
- I ran the held-out split once early (on c8) by mistake. Nothing was chosen from it, and I added a separate "long" case to the tuning inputs instead.

Everything is in `dedup/`: the per-candidate log is in `log.md`, and the harness is `harness.py` with the A/B timer in `ab.py`.
